case_study_insert.main_stem: Pinecrest Dental Practice (PDP) is a private limited company in the healthcare sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2011 by Dr Amina Farouk, it provides general and cosmetic dentistry to local patients and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. PDP plans to invest $540,000 in a second surgery with digital imaging equipment, financed by a $300,000 ten-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $35 a unit and a selling price of $95, and carries out 14,000 units of dental treatment a year. PDP faces two problems: staff absenteeism has reached 8% and patient complaints about appointment waiting times are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The practice completed 3,450 patient appointments last quarter; the did-not-attend rate was 12%, down from 15% a year ago. Patient complaints about waiting times rose from 18 to 29 per month. Average appointment turnaround was 26 minutes. A survey of 500 registered patients found that 68% would pay $8 more for evening appointments, and 57% wanted online booking; the local college charges $650 per staff member for a customer-care course.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Pinecrest Dental Practice for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 4.9%, increasing borrowing costs for practices with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.2% to $14.10 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for clinical and reception staff. (3) Private dental insurance reimbursement rates have been cut by 6.5% while demand for private treatment grew 2.8%; dental materials input costs have risen 9.3% year-on-year.

questions.question_text: PDP plans to fund part of its new surgery with retained profit rather than the $300,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for PDP of using retained profit to finance the expansion.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using the $240,000 of retained profit costs PDP no interest payments or capital repayments, which protects its cash flow and its $480,000 a year fixed-cost base. Unlike the $300,000 ten-year bank loan, there is no monthly debt service to find from the 14,000 units of dental treatment, so every dollar earned can be ploughed back into the second surgery rather than paid to the lender. This matters while patient complaints about waiting times are rising and Dr Amina Farouk still needs cash to hire reception cover.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral risk and keeps ownership with Dr Farouk. The $300,000 bank loan could require the practice's assets or the founder's guarantee as security, putting the existing surgery at risk if the digital imaging equipment fails to attract enough patients. Using $240,000 of past profits avoids that exposure, imposes no lender conditions on how the second surgery is run, and preserves the democratic leadership's freedom to respond to the 8% absenteeism problem without consulting an external bank.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to PDP's expansion, costs and ownership.

questions.question_text: PDP wants to attract patients to its new second surgery. Consider local radio advertising, social media promotions, or referral links with nearby GP surgeries. Which should PDP choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio advertising: Radio reaches commuters across the practice's local catchment cheaply and suits time-limited messages such as a new surgery opening. It is far less costly than television, so it will not strain a business already committing $540,000 to the expansion and servicing a $300,000 loan. However, radio is untargeted: many listeners do not need dentistry, and it cannot convey the digital imaging message visually, so the 3,450 patients already attending and the 500 surveyed patients are not specifically reached.

Social media promotions: Targeted posts can reach exactly the patients identified in the survey — the 68% who would pay $8 more for evening appointments and the 57% who want online booking — at low cost and with immediate measurement. Posts can show the new imaging equipment directly and drive online booking. The drawback is that results depend on constant content, and older patients who may need cosmetic work might be missed by a purely digital channel.

Referral links with GP surgeries: Formal links with nearby GP practices would deliver a steady stream of referred patients with high trust and low marketing cost, and would help fill the second surgery's appointment book quickly, reducing the 12% did-not-attend rate through personal recommendation. Referrals take time to establish and depend on GPs' willingness to cooperate, and volumes may be too slow to cover the $480,000 fixed costs in the first year.

Recommendation: PDP should choose social media promotions. They reach the precise, research-identified segment, are affordable alongside the $540,000 investment, and can be built around the 68% premium for evening appointments and 57% demand for online booking. Radio is rejected as untargeted and wasteful; GP referrals are rejected as too slow to fill capacity quickly, though they should be developed later as a supplement.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with little application to PDP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of PDP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of PDP with a well-justified recommendation and clear rejection of the alternatives.

questions.question_text: PDP's staff absenteeism has reached 8%. Explain two benefits for PDP of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its 40-strong team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives PDP's 40 staff a real say in how the new second surgery and digital imaging equipment are introduced, which helps satisfy esteem and social needs (Maslow) and raises job satisfaction. Receptionists and nurses who help design the appointment schedule are more likely to turn up reliably, directly tackling the 8% absenteeism rate that is disrupting the 3,450 patient appointments completed last quarter.

Point 2: Consulting the team generates practical ideas from the people who handle patients every day, so waiting-time complaints can be reduced and the 12% did-not-attend rate addressed through better reminder routines. Higher involvement builds commitment, lowering labour turnover and avoiding the $650 per staff member cost of replacement customer-care training at the local college, while protecting the output of 14,000 units as the new surgery beds in. Because the $540,000 expansion also brings digital imaging, staff involvement helps them accept new routines rather than resist them, so absence does not climb further.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to PDP's absenteeism, complaints and training costs.

questions.question_text: PDP must train reception staff to use the new online booking system; 57% of surveyed patients want it. Consider on-the-job coaching or the $650-per-person customer-care course at the local college. Which should PDP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job coaching: Training at the reception desk is specific to PDP's own booking system and appointment routines, costs no course fees, and keeps staff productive while they learn, protecting the 3,450 patient appointments handled each quarter and the effort behind falling did-not-attend rates. Its weakness is that the trainer is another receptionist whose own work suffers, bad habits can spread, and there is no recognised certificate, which may matter if patients expect formal service standards.

College course: The $650 per staff member customer-care course at the local college gives structured, up-to-date skills and a certificate. For a handful of receptionists the total cost is small against the $540,000 expansion, and it covers communication skills that could reduce the 29 monthly waiting-time complaints. However, it removes staff from the desk, cutting short-term capacity when the second surgery is opening, and the generic content may not match PDP's exact software, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: PDP should choose on-the-job coaching first, backed by short college sessions for senior receptionists. Coaching is cheaper, system-specific and avoids losing reception cover while absenteeism is 8% and complaints are rising; the full college course is rejected as disruptive and only partly relevant, though the $650 certificate is worth adding once the new booking system has settled and the 57% patient demand can be met reliably. Better telephone manners from the course could also help with the 29 monthly waiting-time complaints, giving a second reason to revisit the college option for reception staff once the second surgery opens.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to PDP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of PDP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of PDP with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how PDP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $480,000 ÷ ($95 − $35) = $480,000 ÷ $60 = 8,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 8,000 units of dental treatment a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $95 − $35 = $60. Answer: contribution per unit is $60.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways PDP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 8,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 14,000 units to confirm the practice is profitable, giving a margin of safety of 6,000 units that shows how far the new second surgery can absorb a dip in patient numbers.
2. Use the $60 contribution per unit to model pricing, for example a $5 discount off the $95 selling price would leave $55 contribution, letting managers judge if extra evening appointments still cover the $480,000 fixed costs.
3. Use the $480,000 fixed costs and $60 contribution to set the volume target needed to service the $300,000 bank loan and justify the $540,000 investment to Dr Farouk before committing further capital.
4. Use average total cost ($480,000 ÷ 14,000 units + $35 = $34.29 + $35 = $69.29 a unit) to benchmark the two surgeries and identify whether rising 9.3% materials costs are pushing unit cost up, so the $35 variable cost can be renegotiated.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 8,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $60 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 6,000 units against 14,000-unit output; discount pricing from $95 using $60 contribution; loan-service volume for the $300,000 loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $69.29 to tackle materials inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate PDP's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has PDP's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: In 2024 a gross profit of $800,000 on revenue of $2,000,000 gives 40.0%; in 2025 $1,080,000 on $2,400,000 gives 45.0%. Operating profit of $250,000 against $2,000,000 revenue gives 12.5% in 2024, and $360,000 against $2,400,000 gives 15.0% in 2025. Operating profit of $250,000 against capital employed of $1,250,000 gives 20.0% in 2024, and $360,000 against $1,600,000 gives 22.5% in 2025.

Evaluation: Every measure moved favourably. The gross margin rose from 40.0% to 45.0%, suggesting better control of clinical supply costs or a richer mix of cosmetic work. The operating margin improved from 12.5% to 15.0%, so overheads including the $480,000 fixed costs were absorbed more effectively as revenue grew. The return on capital employed rose from 20.0% to 22.5%, meaning the $1,250,000 to $1,600,000 asset base is generating more operating profit, which supports the case for the $540,000 second surgery. Interest payable increased only from $30,000 to $35,000, so financing charges are not the cause. However, the return on capital still depends on continuing demand: a 12% did-not-attend rate or the 8% absenteeism could quickly reverse the trend, and the improved ratios are compared with a 2024 base that may have been weak.

Conclusion: PDP's profitability has clearly improved — both margins and the return on capital rose together, and the rise is not explained by accounting adjustments. Priority now is to protect the 45.0% gross margin against 9.3% materials inflation and fill the second surgery so the improvement continues.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation and a justified conclusion on whether profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for PDP of introducing the online booking system wanted by 57% of surveyed patients.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Online booking directly meets the 57% of the 500 surveyed patients who want it and supports the 68% who would pay $8 more for evening appointments, letting PDP fill the new second surgery's diary outside working hours and raise revenue without adding fixed costs. It also cuts the 12% did-not-attend rate through automatic reminders, protecting the 14,000 units of dental treatment and helping absorb the $480,000 a year fixed-cost base.

Disadvantage: Setting up and maintaining online booking needs investment and staff training — the local college charges $650 per person for customer-care training — just as PDP is funding a $540,000 expansion. Patients who are less comfortable with technology could be excluded, and if the system is not kept up to date it may create double bookings, worsening the patient complaints about waiting times rather than solving them. With 3,450 patient appointments already handled each quarter, any double booking would be felt immediately.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to PDP's survey, costs and appointment problems.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.9%, the 5.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.3% rise in dental materials costs will affect PDP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 4.9%): If PDP's $300,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, a 0.65 percentage-point rise adds 0.0065 × $300,000 = $1,950 a year, which is small beside the $480,000 fixed costs and can be largely removed by fixing the rate. Higher rates may also make consumers more cautious about discretionary cosmetic dentistry, but the direct cash effect on the practice is modest.

Minimum wage increase (5.2%, to $14.10 an hour): With a workforce of 40 covering clinical and reception roles, this feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can honestly be invented; the defensible comparison is productivity of 14,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 350 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable through the $60 contribution per unit; if absenteeism at 8% pulls it down, unit labour costs climb and the $480,000 overhead burden becomes harder to cover.

Materials inflation (9.3% dental materials): The insert does not split the $35 variable cost, so only a bound can be computed: if all of it rose 9.3%, that is 0.093 × $35 = $3.26 per unit, or about $45,600 a year at 14,000 units, cutting contribution per unit from $60 toward $56.74. The 6.5% reimbursement cut compounds this on insured work, though 2.8% demand growth and the survey's 68% willing to pay $8 more offer partial recovery.

Conclusion: The 9.3% rise in dental materials costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on all 14,000 units and directly erodes the $60 contribution that justifies the $540,000 expansion, and it is reinforced by the 6.5% reimbursement cut. The loan-rate rise is small and hedgeable; the wage rise is significant but manageable while productivity stays at 350 units per worker.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to PDP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on PDP's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of PDP with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement and reasons for rejecting the others.
